newsitem.title: USA: Spec liquidation continues to batter CSCE cocoa.
newsitem.headline: Spec liquidation continues to batter CSCE cocoa.

text.p: CSCE cocoa futures ended sharply lower and near the bottom of the day's range for the third day in a row on Wednesday, pressured by continued speculative long liquidation, dealers said.

Benchmark September cocoa fell $25 per tonne on the day, to $1,458, after ranging between $1,488 and $1,458. Second-month December also closed $25 lower, at $1,504, while the back months ended down $24 to $25.

Cocoa prices briefly rose in early going, in line with gains overnight in London. Traders said September's inability to get past chart resistance at $1,490 dampened sentiment and helped spark the reversal.
Continued strength in the U.S. dollar against sterling and other European currencies also weighed on the market, they said, and prompted some arbitrage selling in the morning.
"The sterling was down three cents (versus the dollar) and that hurt us," said one trader. "It limited the market to the upside."
Traders said today's activity mirrored the market's pattern over the last two session, with speculators liquidating into steady manufacturer-related and trade buying.
"There seems to be good scale-down buying, but it's not holding the market from coming off," said one dealer.
This week, September cocoa has shed $59 -- or about four percent -- and while some traders noted the market appeared to be oversold, other traders said further losses would not be a surprise.
"I'm not even going to try to pick a bottom anymore," said one trader. "The longs are spooked and they keep liquidating."
On the charts, traders said September now faced support at $1,450, followed by $1,438-$1,436. On the upside, resistance was still seen near $1,475.
While no new fundamentals were seen behind today's sell-off, traders said reports this week of rains in late July favoring Ivorian crop prospects for 1997/98 season continued to weigh on sentiment.
"There's been stories of decent rain and soil moisture -- enough for people to say the next estimate will be revised up," said one trader. "I think they are trying to price in a higher estimate."
